title: Find the footage that matters
description: Move from a broad recording search to the right moment, its surrounding context and safe evidence preservation.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Our fictional warehouse team needs to review something near the loading entrance yesterday afternoon. There are hundreds of clips. Where should the operator begin?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Begin with the day and location, then select the relevant devices and a short time window. The filters narrow the complete result set, not just the cards currently loaded. Add analysis filters when you know what observation you're seeking.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And if the grid suddenly becomes empty?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Check the combined filters before assuming footage is missing. Remove the analysis conditions first to establish whether the camera recorded anything. A copied search link preserves the question, but another person still needs access to its recordings.

chapters.title: A card is a doorway into detail

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: We've found a promising recording. Should the operator immediately leave the search?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Not necessarily. Play in the grid, use available preview frames and positioned marker icons, or open the side panel without losing your search. The full detail page gives more room for video, metadata and available analysis.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What if the clip appears before its thumbnail or detection boxes?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Those are separate processing outputs. They may arrive later or not run in that deployment. Some installations initially register metadata while the video stays at the source, so an eligible recording may need forwarding before playback becomes available.

chapters.title: See what happened before and after

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The warehouse event starts just before this clip. Can we investigate the lead-up without guessing which file comes next?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use the context player to review surrounding footage on an aligned timeline. Narrow the devices and interval so the comparison stays understandable. A gap means no recording is available for that camera at that position.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And the Live tab isn't another way to replay that historical moment?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Correct. Live shows the camera now, not the past incident. Also check the selection before taking an action in the context player: it can apply to the surrounding set, not just the original recording card.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The operator stars the clip and adds a description. Is the incident now safely archived?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Stars and notes help you find and understand a recording; ordinary retention still applies. Use a case for evidence that needs preservation, review the selected media, and confirm archiving succeeds rather than assuming a submitted request has finished.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we remember when passing the investigation on?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Check who can access the footage and which actions their role allows. Search links and copied video links aren't permanent archives or permission grants. Start with a focused search, inspect the context, then choose the appropriate case or sharing workflow.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
